0.title: Zechariah: Behold, Your King Is Coming

1.text: <sup>1</sup>In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,<sup>2</sup>"The LORD was very angry with your fathers.<sup>3</sup>Therefore say to them, Thus declares the LORD of hosts: Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts.<sup>4</sup>Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.' But they did not hear or pay attention to me, declares the LORD.<sup>5</sup>Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?<sup>6</sup>But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? So they repented and said, 'As the LORD of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us.'"<sup>7</sup>On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,<sup>8</sup>"I saw in the night, and behold, a man riding on a red horse! He was standing among the myrtle trees in the glen, and behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses.<sup>9</sup>Then I said, 'What are these, my lord?' The angel who talked with me said to me, 'I will show you what they are.'<sup>10</sup>So the man who was standing among the myrtle trees answered, 'These are they whom the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.'<sup>11</sup>And they answered the angel of the LORD who was standing among the myrtle trees, and said, 'We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth remains at rest.'<sup>12</sup>Then the angel of the LORD said, 'O LORD of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry these seventy years?'<sup>13</sup>And the LORD answered gracious and comforting words to the angel who talked with me.<sup>14</sup>So the angel who talked with me said to me, 'Cry out, Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion.<sup>15</sup>And I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster.<sup>16</sup>Therefore, thus says the LORD, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy; my house shall be built in it, declares the LORD of hosts, and the measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.<sup>17</sup>Cry out again, Thus says the LORD of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and the LORD will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem.'"<sup>18</sup>And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns!<sup>19</sup>And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these?" And he said to me, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem."<sup>20</sup>Then the LORD showed me four craftsmen.<sup>21</sup>And I said, "What are these coming to do?" He said, "These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one raised his head. And these have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations who lifted up their horns against the land of Judah to scatter it."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two months after Haggai began, the word comes to Zechariah: The LORD was very angry with your fathers (vv. 1-2). So, Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you (v. 3). Do not be like the fathers who would not listen (v. 4): Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever? (v. 5). God's words outlived them all, and in the end the exiles admitted he had been right (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: God's call to a new generation is to learn from the last one, because his word outlives everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying, "The LORD was very angry with your fathers. Therefore say to them, Thus declares the LORD of hosts: Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts.
verseByVerse.commentary:
In the eighth month, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,

Zechariah began to preach in 520 BC, two months after Haggai (Hag 1:1), in the same small, discouraged community rebuilding the temple. Ezra names them together: the prophets, Haggai and Zechariah (Ezra 5:1). Haggai was the site foreman, urging the work on. Zechariah is the visionary, lifting their eyes to what God is doing behind the scenes and centuries ahead.

"The LORD was very angry with your fathers.

He starts with history, and it is not comfortable. The exile was not an accident of politics; it was the anger of God against a persistently unfaithful generation.

Therefore say to them, Thus declares the LORD of hosts: Return to me, says the LORD of hosts, and I will return to you, says the LORD of hosts.

Here is the heart of the chapter, and it is an invitation: Return to me ... and I will return to you. Notice the order. God does not say "clean yourselves up and then come". He says come, and I will come. Malachi would repeat it (Mal 3:7), and James puts it in New Testament words: Draw near to God, and he will draw near to you (Jas 4:8).

Notice also the triple says the LORD of hosts in one verse. This is not a suggestion from a prophet; it is the word of the commander of the armies of heaven.

And notice how personal the promise is. God does not merely offer to restore their fortunes or rebuild their walls; he offers himself. That is always the best thing God gives.

verseByVerse.quote: Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.' But they did not hear or pay attention to me, declares the LORD. Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever? But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? So they repented and said, 'As the LORD of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Do not be like your fathers, to whom the former prophets cried out, 'Thus says the LORD of hosts, Return from your evil ways and from your evil deeds.' But they did not hear or pay attention to me, declares the LORD.

Every generation has the chance to be different from the last. The people Zechariah addressed had inherited the wreckage of their grandparents' choices, and the warning is that inheriting the consequences does not automatically mean learning the lesson.

Your fathers, where are they? And the prophets, do they live forever?

Two blunt questions. The fathers are dead. The prophets are dead too. Everyone in that argument is gone.

But my words and my statutes, which I commanded my servants the prophets, did they not overtake your fathers? So they repented and said, 'As the LORD of hosts purposed to deal with us for our ways and deeds, so has he dealt with us.'"

And there is the point: the generations pass, and God's words remain and overtake people. The word is pictured as a pursuer that catches up in the end.

The last line is remarkable. In exile, the fathers finally admitted that God had been right all along: so has he dealt with us. It is a grim way to be persuaded. Zechariah's hearers are being invited to believe God's word now, rather than being convinced by its fulfilment later.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–17 — The Horseman Among the Myrtles
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In a night vision a rider on a red horse stands among the myrtle trees, with horses behind him (vv. 7-8). They have patrolled the earth and report that all the earth remains at rest (vv. 9-11). The angel of the LORD asks, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem? (v. 12), and God answers with gracious and comforting words: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy, and the city will be rebuilt (vv. 13-17).
verseByVerse.theology: When the world is comfortable and God's people are not, God is neither asleep nor indifferent.

verseByVerse.quote: On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying, "I saw in the night, and behold, a man riding on a red horse! He was standing among the myrtle trees in the glen, and behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses. Then I said, 'What are these, my lord?' The angel who talked with me said to me, 'I will show you what they are.' So the man who was standing among the myrtle trees answered, 'These are they whom the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.' And they answered the angel of the LORD who was standing among the myrtle trees, and said, 'We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth remains at rest.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
On the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month, which is the month of Shebat, in the second year of Darius, the word of the LORD came to the prophet Zechariah, the son of Berechiah, son of Iddo, saying,

Three months later comes a series of eight night visions, running through to chapter 6. They are strange, vivid and hopeful, and they were given to people working on a building site with very little to encourage them.

"I saw in the night, and behold, a man riding on a red horse! He was standing among the myrtle trees in the glen, and behind him were red, sorrel, and white horses.

The first vision: a rider on a red horse among the myrtle trees, low bushy trees in a glen, with other horses behind. The scene is quiet, shadowed, ordinary. God's activity is usually hidden in exactly this way.

Then I said, 'What are these, my lord?' The angel who talked with me said to me, 'I will show you what they are.'

Zechariah asks. Through these visions he keeps asking, and he is never rebuked for it. Honest questions are welcome.

So the man who was standing among the myrtle trees answered, 'These are they whom the LORD has sent to patrol the earth.'

And they answered the angel of the LORD who was standing among the myrtle trees, and said, 'We have patrolled the earth, and behold, all the earth remains at rest.'

These riders are God's patrol, sent to survey the world, like a king's scouts reporting back. God is not uninformed about what is happening in Persia or anywhere else.

Their report sounds like good news: all the earth remains at rest. In fact it is the problem. The great empires are comfortable and secure, while God's people are struggling in a ruined city. Haggai had promised that God would shake the nations (Hag 2:6-7), and nothing is shaking.

Believers know this feeling. The wicked appear untroubled, the church is small and tired, and heaven seems quiet. That is exactly the moment the next verse addresses.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the angel of the LORD said, 'O LORD of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry these seventy years?' And the LORD answered gracious and comforting words to the angel who talked with me. So the angel who talked with me said to me, 'Cry out, Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the angel of the LORD said, 'O LORD of hosts, how long will you have no mercy on Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, against which you have been angry these seventy years?'

Now something astonishing: the how long prayer is prayed in heaven, by the angel of the LORD. The question the exiles had been asking for seventy years is taken up and put to God by one who stands in his presence.

The seventy years were the span Jeremiah had foretold for the exile (Jer 25:11; 29:10). God keeps his calendar precisely, even when his people cannot see the clock.

Christians have a better intercessor still. Christ always lives to make intercession for us, and the Spirit prays within us when we do not know what to ask.

And the LORD answered gracious and comforting words to the angel who talked with me.

Four words worth holding: gracious and comforting words. That is God's answer to the how-long prayer.

Anyone praying through a long disappointment should hold that phrase. The answer, when it came, was not a rebuke for asking.

verseByVerse.quote: And I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster. Therefore, thus says the LORD, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy; my house shall be built in it, declares the LORD of hosts, and the measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem. Cry out again, Thus says the LORD of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and the LORD will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
So the angel who talked with me said to me, 'Cry out, Thus says the LORD of hosts: I am exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem and for Zion.

And I am exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease; for while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster.

God is exceedingly jealous for his people, with the fierce protectiveness of a husband, and exceedingly angry with the nations that are at ease. That comfortable calm of verse 11 has not escaped his notice.

The charge against those nations is precise: while I was angry but a little, they furthered the disaster. God used them to discipline his people, and they went far beyond the brief, enjoying the destruction. Being an instrument in God's hand is no excuse for cruelty.

Therefore, thus says the LORD, I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy; my house shall be built in it, declares the LORD of hosts, and the measuring line shall be stretched out over Jerusalem.

Cry out again, Thus says the LORD of hosts: My cities shall again overflow with prosperity, and the LORD will again comfort Zion and again choose Jerusalem.'"

The promise answers verse 3. They were told Return to me; now God says I have returned to Jerusalem with mercy. A measuring line comes out, which is what builders do when they intend to build. And three times again: prosperity again, comfort again, chosen again.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 18–21 — Four Horns and Four Craftsmen
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zechariah sees four horns, the powers that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem (vv. 18-19), and then four craftsmen who have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: For every power that scatters God's people, God has a workman ready to break it.

verseByVerse.quote: And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns! And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these?" And he said to me, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem." Then the LORD showed me four craftsmen. And I said, "What are these coming to do?" He said, "These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one raised his head. And these have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations who lifted up their horns against the land of Judah to scatter it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, four horns!

(In the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 2, as the ESV notes.) A horn in the Bible pictures power, as the horn of a bull is its strength. Four of them stand for power in every direction.

And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these?" And he said to me, "These are the horns that have scattered Judah, Israel, and Jerusalem."

These are the empires and armies that have battered God's people over centuries. Zechariah does not name them, and neither should we press the number into a list of four specific kingdoms. The point is completeness: every power that ever scattered them.

Then the LORD showed me four craftsmen.

And I said, "What are these coming to do?" He said, "These are the horns that scattered Judah, so that no one raised his head. And these have come to terrify them, to cast down the horns of the nations who lifted up their horns against the land of Judah to scatter it."

And here is the comfort of the vision. For every horn there is a craftsman: a workman with tools, come to cut the horns off. The number matches exactly. God is never one short.

Notice the detail so that no one raised his head. That is what oppression does; it makes people look at the ground. And God's answer is not a sermon about keeping your chin up. It is workmen.

History bears this out. Assyria fell to Babylon, Babylon to Persia, and every power that ever crushed God's people has in time been broken by another. Behind that sequence stands the God who commissions craftsmen. And at the end of the story the last enemy, death itself, is destroyed by the carpenter from Nazareth.

1.title: Return to Me, and I Will Return to You
1.overview:
In the second year of Darius the word of the LORD comes to Zechariah. God was very angry with their fathers, so he calls this generation: "Return to me, and I will return to you." They are not to be like the fathers who ignored the former prophets. The fathers are dead and so are the prophets, but God's words overtook them, and in the end they admitted that God had dealt with them exactly as he purposed (vv. 1-6).

Three months later, in a night vision, Zechariah sees a man on a red horse among the myrtle trees with horses behind him. They are God's patrol, and they report that all the earth remains at rest (vv. 7-11). The angel of the LORD asks how long God will withhold mercy from Jerusalem after seventy years, and God answers with gracious and comforting words: he is exceedingly jealous for Jerusalem, exceedingly angry with the nations at ease who furthered the disaster, and has returned to Jerusalem with mercy; his house will be built and the measuring line stretched out, and his cities will again overflow with prosperity (vv. 12-17).

Then he sees four horns, the powers that scattered Judah, Israel and Jerusalem, and four craftsmen who have come to terrify them and cast down those horns (vv. 18-21).
1.theology:
God's call to return comes with a promise that he will return, and the initiative is his (v. 3; Mal 3:7; Jas 4:8).

Each generation must respond for itself; inheriting the consequences of sin is not the same as learning from it (vv. 4-6).

God's word outlives every generation and overtakes those who ignore it (v. 6).

God patrols and knows the whole earth; the comfort of the nations is not hidden from him (vv. 10-11, 15).

God keeps his own calendar exactly, even when his people cannot see the clock (v. 12; Jer 29:10).

God is jealous for his people with a husband's protectiveness, and answers their "how long" with gracious and comforting words (vv. 13-14).

Being used by God as an instrument of discipline excuses no one's cruelty (v. 15).

For every power that scatters God's people, God has a craftsman ready to break it (vv. 20-21).
1.examples:
A prophet of visions preaching alongside a prophet of scaffolding.

Two questions: where are the fathers, and where are the prophets?

God's word pictured as a pursuer that overtakes people in the end.

Horsemen reporting that the world is quiet, which is the problem.

A "how long?" prayer prayed in heaven.

A measuring line taken out over a ruined city.

Four horns, and exactly four workmen with tools.

And he said to me, "To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its width and what is its length."<sup>3</sup>And behold, the angel who talked with me came forward, and another angel came forward to meet him<sup>4</sup>and said to him, "Run, say to that young man, 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it.<sup>5</sup>And I will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory in her midst.'"<sup>6</sup>Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, declares the LORD. For I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heavens, declares the LORD.<sup>7</sup>Up! Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.<sup>8</sup>For thus said the LORD of hosts, after his glory sent me to the nations who plundered you, for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye:<sup>9</sup>"Behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they shall become plunder for those who served them. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me.<sup>10</sup>Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst, declares the LORD.<sup>11</sup>And many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people. And I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you.<sup>12</sup>And the LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land, and will again choose Jerusalem."<sup>13</sup>Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A man goes out with a measuring line in his hand to measure Jerusalem (vv. 1-2), and is stopped: Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it (vv. 3-4). God himself will be her defence and her glory: I will be to her a wall of fire all around ... and I will be the glory in her midst (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: God's plans for his people are larger than their plans, and his protection is better than their walls.

verseByVerse.quote: And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand! Then I said, "Where are you going?" And he said to me, "To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its width and what is its length." And behold, the angel who talked with me came forward, and another angel came forward to meet him and said to him, "Run, say to that young man, 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it. And I will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory in her midst.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
And I lifted my eyes and saw, and behold, a man with a measuring line in his hand!

Then I said, "Where are you going?" And he said to me, "To measure Jerusalem, to see what is its width and what is its length."

(In the Hebrew Bible this chapter begins at 2:5, as the ESV notes.) The third night vision begins with a sensible man doing a sensible thing. Jerusalem needs rebuilding, so somebody takes a measuring line to work out the size of the walls.

And behold, the angel who talked with me came forward, and another angel came forward to meet him

and said to him, "Run, say to that young man, 'Jerusalem shall be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it.

An angel is sent running to stop him. The surveyor is thinking about a wall; God is thinking about a crowd. There will be too many people to fit inside any wall he could draw, so the city will spread out as villages without walls.

This is a word for every believer whose plans for God's work are too small. We measure what we can manage. God plans for what he intends to give.

And I will be to her a wall of fire all around, declares the LORD, and I will be the glory in her midst.'"

But a city without walls is defenceless, which is why they wanted walls in the first place. God's answer is one of the great promises of the Old Testament: I will be to her a wall of fire all around. Shepherds lit fires around the flock at night to keep predators off. God himself will be that ring of fire.

And more: I will be the glory in her midst. The old temple had held the visible glory of God, and it had gone. God promises to be the glory himself, at the centre of his people.

Put the two halves together and you have the church's security in any age: God around us and God among us. A congregation with no buildings, no money and no influence has these.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — The Apple of His Eye
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, God calls to those still in Babylon (vv. 6-7). Of the nations that plundered his people he says, he who touches you touches the apple of his eye, and they will become plunder themselves (vv. 8-9).
verseByVerse.theology: To touch God's people is to touch the most sensitive part of God.

verseByVerse.quote: Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, declares the LORD. For I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heavens, declares the LORD. Up! Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon. For thus said the LORD of hosts, after his glory sent me to the nations who plundered you, for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye: "Behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they shall become plunder for those who served them. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up! Up! Flee from the land of the north, declares the LORD. For I have spread you abroad as the four winds of the heavens, declares the LORD.

Up! Escape to Zion, you who dwell with the daughter of Babylon.

Many Jews had stayed in Babylon when the exiles were allowed home. Life there was settled and comfortable, and Jerusalem was a building site. God's call is urgent: Up! Up! Come home.

There is a pattern here that repeats through Scripture. God's people can be so comfortable in the place of exile that they need to be called out of it, and the call is always to where God is at work rather than to where life is easiest.

For thus said the LORD of hosts, after his glory sent me to the nations who plundered you, for he who touches you touches the apple of his eye:

Here is one of the tenderest phrases in the Bible. (The ESV notes the first line may read "he sent me after glory".) The apple of his eye means the pupil, the most sensitive and most fiercely protected part of the body. Touch a person's eye and their whole body reacts instantly. Moses used the same picture of God's care for Israel in the desert (Deut 32:10), and David prayed it: Keep me as the apple of your eye (Ps 17:8).

So anyone who harms God's people is not merely offending an institution. They have poked God in the eye. Jesus said the same to a man persecuting the church: Saul, Saul, why are you persecuting me? (Acts 9:4).

"Behold, I will shake my hand over them, and they shall become plunder for those who served them. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me.

The reversal is complete: the plunderers become the plunder, and the slaves take the spoil. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me. The speaker is sent by the LORD of hosts and yet speaks as the LORD; Christians, reading with the New Testament open, recognise the pattern that becomes clear when the Son is sent by the Father.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–13 — I Will Dwell in Your Midst
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst (v. 10). Many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people (v. 11), and God will again choose Jerusalem (v. 12). Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: God's answer to a small, frightened community is that he is coming to live among them, and to gather the nations with them.

verseByVerse.quote: Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst, declares the LORD. And many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people. And I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. And the LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land, and will again choose Jerusalem." Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Sing and rejoice, O daughter of Zion, for behold, I come and I will dwell in your midst, declares the LORD.

This is the summit of the vision. Not "I will protect you from a distance" but I come and I will dwell in your midst. The word is the language of pitching a tent among them, as God did in the wilderness.

John opens his Gospel with exactly this promise fulfilled: the Word became flesh and dwelt among us, and we have seen his glory (John 1:14). And the Bible ends with it complete: Behold, the dwelling place of God is with man (Rev 21:3). A small community rebuilding a temple is told that God intends to come and live with them, and that promise ran all the way to Bethlehem and beyond.

And many nations shall join themselves to the LORD in that day, and shall be my people. And I will dwell in your midst, and you shall know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you.

And the family will be far larger than they imagined: many nations shall join themselves to the LORD ... and shall be my people. The phrase "my people" had belonged to Israel alone. Now it is being handed out to the nations. That is the gospel arriving in advance, and every Gentile Christian is part of the fulfilment.

And the LORD will inherit Judah as his portion in the holy land, and will again choose Jerusalem."

God will take Judah as his own portion, the word used for an inheritance. His people are his treasure, not merely his responsibility.

Be silent, all flesh, before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling.

The chapter ends with a hush. Be silent, all flesh: the same command Habakkuk and Zephaniah gave (Hab 2:20; Zeph 1:7). All the noisy powers of the world have nothing to say now.

And the reason is wonderful: he has roused himself from his holy dwelling. God has stood up. To a people who wondered whether heaven was asleep (1:11), this is the answer: he is awake, he is moving, and the right response is awed silence.

2.title: A Wall of Fire All Around
2.overview:
Zechariah sees a man going out with a measuring line to measure Jerusalem, and an angel runs to tell him that Jerusalem will be inhabited as villages without walls, because of the multitude of people and livestock in it. God himself will be a wall of fire around her and the glory in her midst (vv. 1-5).

God calls those still in Babylon to flee the land of the north and escape to Zion, for he had scattered them like the four winds (vv. 6-7). Of the nations that plundered them he says that whoever touches them touches the apple of his eye; he will shake his hand over them, and they will become plunder for those who served them (vv. 8-9).

Zion is told to sing and rejoice, for God is coming to dwell in her midst; many nations will join themselves to the LORD and become his people, and he will inherit Judah and again choose Jerusalem (vv. 10-12). Let all flesh be silent before the LORD, for he has roused himself from his holy dwelling (v. 13).
2.theology:
God's plans for his people are larger than the plans they make for themselves (vv. 2-4).

God himself is the security and the glory of his people, which is better than any wall (v. 5).

God calls his people out of comfortable exile to where he is working (vv. 6-7).

Those who harm God's people touch the most sensitive part of God (v. 8; Deut 32:10; Ps 17:8; Acts 9:4).

God's great promise is not distance but presence: he comes to dwell among his people, fulfilled in Christ and completed in the new creation (v. 10; John 1:14; Rev 21:3).

The nations are to be joined to the LORD and called "my people" alongside Israel (v. 11).

When God rouses himself to act, the right response of all flesh is silence (v. 13; Hab 2:20; Zeph 1:7).
2.examples:
A surveyor measuring for walls, stopped by an angel at a run.

A city that outgrows every boundary anyone could draw for it.

A shepherd's ring of fire, and God saying he will be it.

Exiles too comfortable in Babylon to come home.

The pupil of an eye, and what happens when it is touched.

A promise of God moving in, made to people with a half-built temple.

The whole world told to be quiet because God has stood up.

3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Satan, "The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?"<sup>3</sup>Now Joshua was standing before the angel, clothed with filthy garments.<sup>4</sup>And the angel said to those who were standing before him, "Remove the filthy garments from him." And to him he said, "Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments."<sup>5</sup>And I said, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD was standing by.<sup>6</sup>And the angel of the LORD solemnly assured Joshua,<sup>7</sup>"Thus says the LORD of hosts: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you shall rule my house and have charge of my courts, and I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here.<sup>8</sup>Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign: behold, I will bring my servant the Branch.<sup>9</sup>For behold, on the stone that I have set before Joshua, on a single stone with seven eyes, I will engrave its inscription, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.<sup>10</sup>In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, every one of you will invite his neighbor to come under his vine and under his fig tree."

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him (v. 1). God does not debate: The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! Is not this man a brand plucked from the fire? (v. 2). Joshua stands there clothed with filthy garments (v. 3), and the order comes: Remove the filthy garments from him ... I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments (vv. 4-5).
verseByVerse.theology: God answers the accusation against his people not by denying the filth but by removing it and clothing them himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. And the LORD said to Satan, "The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?" Now Joshua was standing before the angel, clothed with filthy garments.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he showed me Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD, and Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him.

The fourth vision is a courtroom. Joshua the high priest is a real man, the one working alongside Zerubbabel on the temple (Hag 1:1). He is the representative of the whole people before God: when he stands there, they stand there.

And there is a prosecutor: Satan standing at his right hand to accuse him. (The ESV notes the Hebrew means "the Accuser" or "the Adversary".) That is what he does. Revelation calls him the accuser of our brothers ... who accuses them day and night before our God (Rev 12:10).

We should be honest about the accusations. They were not false. The priesthood had failed, the nation had earned its exile, and Joshua had nothing to say. Satan's charges against Christians are usually true too, which is what makes them so effective.

And the LORD said to Satan, "The LORD rebuke you, O Satan! The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! Is not this a brand plucked from the fire?"

God does not answer the accusation with an argument. He silences the accuser: The LORD rebuke you. And the ground of the rebuke is not Joshua's record but God's choice: The LORD who has chosen Jerusalem.

Then a picture that says everything: a brand plucked from the fire (the ESV notes this is a burning stick). Joshua is a half-burnt piece of wood, snatched out of the flames of the exile. He is not impressive. He is rescued, and rescued things belong to their rescuer.

This is the answer to every accusation a believer will ever face. Not "I am better than you say", but "I have been pulled out of the fire by God, and he is the one you are arguing with". Paul puts it as two questions: Who shall bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies (Rom 8:33).

Now Joshua was standing before the angel, clothed with filthy garments.

The Bible does not tidy up the picture. The high priest is standing in God's presence in filthy garments, and the word is a strong one: these are clothes soiled in the most disgusting way. That is how sin looks in heaven's light, and dressing it up helps nobody.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel said to those who were standing before him, "Remove the filthy garments from him." And to him he said, "Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments." And I said, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD was standing by.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel said to those who were standing before him, "Remove the filthy garments from him." And to him he said, "Behold, I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments."

Now watch the order carefully, because it is the gospel.

First, God acts: Remove the filthy garments from him. Joshua does not wash them, or promise to do better, or defend himself. He is stripped by others while he stands there.

Second, God explains: I have taken your iniquity away from you. The clothes were never the problem; the iniquity was, and God says he has taken it. Where it went is not said here. The New Testament tells us: it was laid on Christ, who dealt with it by canceling the record of debt that stood against us, nailing it to the cross (Col 2:14).

Third, God clothes: I will clothe you with pure vestments. God does not leave his people standing naked once the filth is gone. Isaiah sings of it: he has clothed me with the garments of salvation; he has covered me with the robe of righteousness (Isa 61:10). In Revelation the saints wear robes washed in the blood of the Lamb (Rev 7:14).

And I said, "Let them put a clean turban on his head." So they put a clean turban on his head and clothed him with garments. And the angel of the LORD was standing by.

Here Zechariah, watching, cannot keep quiet: Let them put a clean turban on his head. The high priest's turban carried a golden plate engraved "Holy to the LORD". Zechariah wants the man fully restored, not merely cleaned up, and his request is granted.

It is a lovely detail that a spectator's prayer is answered in the middle of a vision. And it is a good instinct for believers watching someone else's restoration: ask for the turban too. Full reinstatement, not grudging tolerance.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua is charged to walk in God's ways, with promise of access among those who are standing here (vv. 6-7). He and his fellow priests are men who are a sign, for God says, behold, I will bring my servant the Branch (v. 8). On a single stone with seven eyes God will engrave an inscription, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day (v. 9) — after which everyone will sit under vine and fig tree (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The cleansing of one priest points to the coming of the Branch, who takes away a nation's guilt in a single day.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel of the LORD solemnly assured Joshua, "Thus says the LORD of hosts: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you shall rule my house and have charge of my courts, and I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here.
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel of the LORD solemnly assured Joshua,

"Thus says the LORD of hosts: If you will walk in my ways and keep my charge, then you shall rule my house and have charge of my courts, and I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here.

After the grace comes the charge. Note the order once more: Joshua is cleansed first and commanded second. The if here is not the condition of his forgiveness but the shape of his service.

Three things are promised. He will rule my house: real responsibility. He will have charge of my courts: real authority. And, best of all, I will give you the right of access among those who are standing here, that is, among the angels in God's presence.

Access is the great privilege. The high priest went into God's presence once a year, trembling. This promises something freer. Christians have it in full: through Christ we have access in one Spirit to the Father, and may draw near with confidence.

verseByVerse.quote: Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign: behold, I will bring my servant the Branch. For behold, on the stone that I have set before Joshua, on a single stone with seven eyes, I will engrave its inscription, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day. In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, every one of you will invite his neighbor to come under his vine and under his fig tree."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hear now, O Joshua the high priest, you and your friends who sit before you, for they are men who are a sign: behold, I will bring my servant the Branch.

Now the vision opens onto something far larger than one priest's restoration. Joshua and his fellow priests are men who are a sign: living signposts pointing beyond themselves.

Pointing to whom? My servant the Branch. Both titles are loaded. My servant is Isaiah's word for the one who would bear his people's iniquities. The Branch is the promised king from David's fallen family tree: I will raise up for David a righteous Branch (Jer 23:5), a shoot from the stump of Jesse (Isa 11:1). Zechariah will use the title again and add something remarkable: this Branch will be both priest and king on one throne (6:12-13).

So the message to a discouraged priest is: you have been cleansed, and one is coming who will do this for everyone.

For behold, on the stone that I have set before Joshua, on a single stone with seven eyes, I will engrave its inscription, declares the LORD of hosts, and I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day.

A mysterious verse. The stone may be a foundation stone of the temple or a jewel on the priest's clothing; the seven eyes (the ESV notes this may mean "facets") suggest either God's complete sight or a stone cut to catch the light. Scripture does not explain it, and we should not pretend to more certainty than the text gives.

What is unmistakable is the last clause: I will remove the iniquity of this land in a single day. Not gradually, not by a lifetime of sacrifices, but in one day. Under the old system the Day of Atonement came round every year, because it never finished the job.

Christians know which day this was. We have been sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all, and by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified (Heb 10:10, 14). What was promised to a man in filthy clothes was accomplished on a Friday afternoon outside Jerusalem.

In that day, declares the LORD of hosts, every one of you will invite his neighbor to come under his vine and under his fig tree."

And the result of forgiveness is neighbourliness. The picture is Micah's: everyone at peace under his vine and his fig tree (Mic 4:4), and here they are inviting each other over.

That is a fine test of whether grace has landed. People who know their own filthy garments have been taken away are not hard to live next door to.

3.title: Filthy Garments and Clean Vestments
3.overview:
Zechariah sees Joshua the high priest standing before the angel of the LORD with Satan at his right hand to accuse him (v. 1). The LORD rebukes Satan, on the ground that he has chosen Jerusalem, and calls Joshua a brand plucked from the fire (v. 2). Joshua stands clothed in filthy garments (v. 3), and the angel orders them removed: "I have taken your iniquity away from you, and I will clothe you with pure vestments." At Zechariah's request a clean turban is put on his head (vv. 4-5).

The angel then charges Joshua: if he walks in God's ways and keeps his charge, he will rule God's house, have charge of his courts, and be given the right of access among those standing there (vv. 6-7). Joshua and his fellow priests are men who are a sign, for God will bring his servant the Branch (v. 8). On a single stone with seven eyes God will engrave an inscription, and he will remove the iniquity of the land in a single day (v. 9); in that day everyone will invite his neighbour under his vine and fig tree (v. 10).
3.theology:
Satan accuses God's people, and his charges are often true (v. 1; Rev 12:10).

God silences accusation not by argument but by his own choice and rescue of his people (v. 2; Rom 8:33-34).

Scripture is honest about how sin looks in God's presence, and God deals with it rather than dressing it up (vv. 3-4).

The order of grace: God removes the filth, takes away the iniquity, and clothes his people himself (v. 4; Isa 61:10; Rev 7:14; Col 2:14).

Cleansing comes first and the charge to serve comes second (vv. 6-7).

Access to God's presence is the great privilege, given fully in Christ (v. 7).

The Branch is the promised servant-king, and the cleansing of one priest is a sign of him (v. 8; Isa 11:1; Jer 23:5; Zech 6:12-13).

Iniquity is removed in a single day, fulfilled at the cross once for all (v. 9; Heb 10:10, 14).
3.examples:
A courtroom where the prosecutor's accusations are all true.

A high priest standing before God in disgusting clothes.

A half-burnt stick pulled out of a fire.

Someone else stripping the filth off a man who cannot do it himself.

A bystander asking for the turban as well, and getting it.

A Day of Atonement that never had to be repeated.

Forgiven neighbours inviting each other under the fig tree.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Lampstand and the Word to Zerubbabel
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Zechariah is woken to see a lampstand all of gold with seven lamps, fed by two olive trees (vv. 1-3). He asks what it means (vv. 4-5), and the answer comes as a word for the governor: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts (v. 6). The obstacle is addressed directly: Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain, and the last stone will go up to shouts of Grace, grace to it! (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: God's work is done by his Spirit, not by human resources, and the finished result is all of grace.

verseByVerse.quote: And the angel who talked with me came again and woke me, like a man who is awakened out of his sleep. And he said to me, "What do you see?" I said, "I see, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, with a bowl on the top of it, and seven lamps on it, with seven lips on each of the lamps that are on the top of it. And there are two olive trees by it, one on the right of the bowl and the other on its left." And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?" Then the angel who talked with me answered and said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord."
verseByVerse.commentary:
And the angel who talked with me came again and woke me, like a man who is awakened out of his sleep.

Zechariah has to be woken. Even a prophet in the middle of a night of visions gets tired. God knows the frailty of his messengers and works round it.

And he said to me, "What do you see?" I said, "I see, and behold, a lampstand all of gold, with a bowl on the top of it, and seven lamps on it, with seven lips on each of the lamps that are on the top of it.

And there are two olive trees by it, one on the right of the bowl and the other on its left."

The fifth vision: a golden lampstand with seven lamps, like the one that had stood in the tabernacle and the temple, but with a difference. This one has a bowl on top and two living olive trees beside it, feeding oil straight into the lamps.

The old lampstand needed priests to carry in the oil each day. This one is supplied without human effort, continuously, from living trees.

And I said to the angel who talked with me, "What are these, my lord?"

Then the angel who talked with me answered and said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord."

Zechariah admits he has no idea. It is a small thing, but a healthy one: he does not invent a meaning. Much confusion in Bible reading comes from being unwilling to say No, my lord.

verseByVerse.quote: Then he said to me, "This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts. Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain. And he shall bring forward the top stone amid shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then he said to me, "This is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts.

The explanation of the vision turns out to be a sentence, and it is one of the best-known in the Bible.

Think who first heard it. Zerubbabel was governor of a province with no army, no treasury and no political weight, trying to rebuild a temple with a handful of discouraged people while neighbouring officials wrote hostile letters to the Persian court. Might and power are exactly what he did not have.

God's answer is not "I will give you might and power". It is but by my Spirit. The lampstand burns because the oil never stops flowing, not because anyone is running to fill it.

This is not a warning against effort; the same chapter says Zerubbabel's own hands will finish the house (v. 9). It is a statement about what actually makes the work go. Churches and Christians can be tempted to believe that what is needed is more resources, better methods or stronger personalities. Those may help, and they are not the power. The temple was finished by the Spirit of God through the hands of ordinary men.

Who are you, O great mountain? Before Zerubbabel you shall become a plain. And he shall bring forward the top stone amid shouts of 'Grace, grace to it!'"

Now the obstacle is addressed to its face, almost with contempt: Who are you, O great mountain? Whatever the mountain was, opposition, poverty, discouragement, it is told that it will be flattened into a plain.

And then the finish: the top stone, the last stone set into a building, brought out to shouts of Grace, grace to it! Not "well done us". When God's work is completed, the only appropriate cheer is about grace, because the whole thing was a gift from beginning to end.

There is a greater building and a greater stone. The psalm sang of The stone that the builders rejected which has become the cornerstone (Ps 118:22), and Jesus applied that verse to himself (Matt 21:42). Peter writes that God laid in Zion a stone, a cornerstone chosen and precious (1 Pet 2:6). When the last stone of God's true temple is set in place, the shout will be the same: grace, grace to it.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Day of Small Things
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it (vv. 8-9). Whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice when they see the plumb line in his hand, for These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth (v. 10). The two olive trees are explained: These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (vv. 11-14).
verseByVerse.theology: God finishes what he starts, delights in small beginnings, and keeps his servants supplied.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying, "The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you. For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. "These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then the word of the LORD came to me, saying,

"The hands of Zerubbabel have laid the foundation of this house; his hands shall also complete it. Then you will know that the LORD of hosts has sent me to you.

A promise every discouraged worker needs: the man who started it will finish it. The foundation had been laid sixteen years before and then abandoned. God says the same pair of hands will set the last stone, and they did; the temple was completed in 516 BC (Ezra 6:15).

God is not in the habit of leaving things half built. Paul says the same about the work God does in a person: he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion.

For whoever has despised the day of small things shall rejoice, and shall see the plumb line in the hand of Zerubbabel. "These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth."

Here is one of the kindest phrases in Scripture: the day of small things. Some had looked at this temple and sneered, as the old men had wept over it (Hag 2:3). God does not scold them for long; he simply says they will end up rejoicing when they see the plumb line in the governor's hand, the ordinary tool of a builder checking his wall.

Most of God's work looks small while it is happening. A handful of people praying, one difficult conversation, a child taught patiently. Despising small days is a real temptation, and it usually means we have mistaken size for significance.

And why will small things not fail? These seven are the eyes of the LORD, which range through the whole earth. The lamps on the lampstand are God's own watchful eyes. Nothing done for him in a back street is unobserved. As Chronicles puts it, the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth, to give strong support to those whose heart is blameless toward him (2 Chr 16:9).

verseByVerse.quote: Then I said to him, "What are these two olive trees on the right and the left of the lampstand?" And a second time I answered and said to him, "What are these two branches of the olive trees, which are beside the two golden pipes from which the golden oil is poured out?" He said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord." Then he said, "These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Then I said to him, "What are these two olive trees on the right and the left of the lampstand?"

And a second time I answered and said to him, "What are these two branches of the olive trees, which are beside the two golden pipes from which the golden oil is poured out?"

Zechariah asks twice, because the first answer did not cover the trees. (The ESV notes the Hebrew does not have the word oil here; it reads simply "the golden".) He wants to know where the supply comes from.

He said to me, "Do you not know what these are?" I said, "No, my lord."

Then he said, "These are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth."

The answer is the two anointed ones (the ESV notes the Hebrew is "two sons of new oil"). In that community there were exactly two anointed offices: Zerubbabel the governor from David's line, and Joshua the high priest. Through these two God was supplying his people: the king's office and the priest's office, keeping the lamp alight.

But notice where they stand: they stand by the Lord of the whole earth. They are servants, not the source. The oil is God's.

And the two offices were never meant to stay apart. Two chapters later Zechariah watches a crown placed on Joshua's head, with the promise that the Branch shall be a priest on his throne (6:13). What took two men in 520 BC is held by one man now. Jesus Christ is king and priest together, and his people are kept burning by his Spirit.

Revelation picks up both images: the churches are lampstands (Rev 1:20), and two witnesses are called the two olive trees and the two lampstands (Rev 11:4). The church's job, then, is not to generate light but to hold it, and to stay connected to the supply.

4.title: Not by Might, nor by Power
4.overview:
The angel wakes Zechariah and asks what he sees: a golden lampstand with a bowl on top, seven lamps, and two olive trees beside it (vv. 1-3). He asks what it means and admits he does not know (vv. 4-5). The answer is the word of the LORD to Zerubbabel: "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit, says the LORD of hosts." The great mountain will become a plain before him, and he will bring out the top stone amid shouts of "Grace, grace to it!" (vv. 6-7).

The hands that laid the foundation of the house will also complete it (vv. 8-9). Whoever despised the day of small things will rejoice to see the plumb line in Zerubbabel's hand, for the seven lamps are the eyes of the LORD ranging through the whole earth (v. 10).

Zechariah asks twice about the two olive trees and the golden pipes pouring out oil, and is told they are the two anointed ones who stand by the Lord of the whole earth (vv. 11-14).
4.theology:
God's work is accomplished by his Spirit rather than by human resources, which does not make human effort unnecessary (vv. 6, 9).

Obstacles that look like mountains are levelled before the purposes of God (v. 7).

When God's work is finished, the only fitting shout is about grace (v. 7).

God completes what he begins (v. 9).

God does not despise small beginnings, and his eyes range over the whole earth to support his people (v. 10; 2 Chr 16:9).

God supplies his people through his appointed servants, who stand by him and are not themselves the source (v. 14).

The offices of king and priest, held by two men here, are united in Christ (v. 14; 6:13).
4.examples:
A prophet who has to be woken up mid-vision.

A lampstand fed by living trees instead of by servants with jars.

A governor with no army told what his real resource is.

A mountain asked, to its face, who it thinks it is.

The last stone of a building greeted with "Grace, grace!"

A builder's plumb line held by hands that finished what they started.

Seven lamps that turn out to be the eyes of God.
